name: Troxell-Steckel House

location.text: 4229 Reliance Street, Egypt, Whitehall Township, Lehigh County, Pennsylvania

dates.altered: Given with the property to the Lehigh County Historical Society in 1942; restored over about thirty years and dedicated as a museum in June 1972; added to the National Register in 1980.
dates.note: A stone inset on the second storey carries the date and, in German, the names of Johan Peter Trochsel and Maria Magdala. Wikipedia states the 1980 listing without printing a reference number, so none is recorded.

refs.title: Troxell-Steckel House - Wikipedia
refs.note: 'Built in 1756 by Johannes Peter Troxell (1719-1799), the historic structure is a 2+1/2-story, fieldstone dwelling with a high-pitched gable roof. Designed in the Pennsylvania-German style, it measures 48 feet (14.6 m) long and 35 feet (10.6 m) wide.' Also on the property: a contributing stone spring house and a late-nineteenth-century barn.

refs.title: Troxell-Steckel House, Whitehall, Lehigh County -- MarkerQuest
refs.note: A marker-hunting blog, recorded as one, but the only source read that gives the siting: Troxell 'purchased a plot of land adjacent to an excellent spring, and in 1756, his work was completed. It's a two-and-a-half story stone house in the German medieval style of architecture; it's made from local fieldstone and timber, measuring 48 feet long and 35 feet wide.'

refs.title: Lehigh County Treasure Trail -- Discover Lehigh Valley (Lehigh County Historical Society property)
refs.note: 'Its location along Coplay Creek and a natural spring made it ideal for farming, with a springhouse used for fresh water and food storage. Once among the largest homes on the frontier.'

note: The plain measurable one. No HABS survey was found under any name tried, so the 48 x 35 ft figure reaches this record through Wikipedia and a marker blog rather than through a survey, and it is recorded as a SECONDARY figure. It is carried because that ratio -- 1.37 -- is the widest in this cluster against the Hans Herr House's 1.22 and the Golden Plough Tavern's 1.20, and because the springhouse is a separate building here where at Fort Zeller and the Hager House the spring runs under the dwelling. That contrast is the whole argument of the bank-house node, drawn between two buildings forty miles apart.
